If it be that my hon. friend- helped the great big millers and helped the great big

contractors out of the hole and did not help the farmers out of the hole, then I just say we have got another piece of evidence to show us which side he is on, with all his fair words. If it be that on that occasion the farmers got no redress from him, but the great millers and the great wheat dealers came here and got his ear and said to him: Lend us this wheat back, and he helped them out of the hole, it shows that his first desire was to serve these people, whose interests, as we say, are always in conflict with those of our con-
5 p.m. stituents and you cannot serve two masters. Whether my information be correct or not, I have this to say; that it is no courtesy to this House, as a gathering of the people's representatives, that when my hon. friend was on his feet for an hour or two he never made the slightest explanation of this very important matter, although he knew all about it, that it had been referred to in the House, and that questions had been asked by different members, particularly by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) long before my, hon. friend addressed the House.
I wish to say a word about this dirty seed grain. Here is a letter which I received last June from Gravelbourg where the municipal authorities rejected a great deal of my hon. friend's seed grain because there were too many weed seeds in it, and I suppose they burned it. The letter is as follows:
Gravelbourg, Sask., June 4, 1915. W. E. Knowles, M.P.,
Moosejaw, Sask.
Dear. Sir,-The following case has been brought to my attention and I wish to communicate the facts to you as the same may furnish an interesting subject for an article in the newspapers.
One H. E. Cork has been sent to Gravelbourg by the Dominion Government to distribute feed grain to the farmers. I take it that the Government sells this grain to the farmers who want it and take a lien on their land as security for the payment of the purchase price.
The grain thus distributed is however of a such poor grade that the weed-inspector of the municipality was compelled to take proceedings against Mr. Cork for disposing of the Dominion Government grain contrary to ' the Noxious Weeds Act of the province.
The case came up on the 29th of May for a hearing before P. N. Aussant, a Justice of the Peace, and Mr. Cork having failed to appear, the evidence on the part of the complainant was heard. Mr. Cork was found guilty and fined $25.00 and costs.
The farmers of this vicinity and more especially the grain growers are greatly disgusted with the work of the Government.
Rural municipalities spend their money yearly, earnestly striving to get rid of the

weeds, and the Government comes along and infests the country with more weeds than ever. Apparently friends of the Government secure contracts to provide the grain for seed purposes, and its seems immaterial whether it is free from weeds or not.
I shall not go further into the matter of the seed grain, but I wish to say a word or two about the collections made by the Government this fall. This fall they got busy. I suppose the Solicitor General was consulted about this. However, they said: We are going to get every dollar we advanced from the farmers of the West, no matter whether we leave them without coal and ishoes for the kiddies, or food to eat, or dresses to wear. Mr. J. Bruce Walker, for the Minister of the Interior-I wish the minister was in his seat, he is away a very great deal, I am sorry to say, but perhaps he will be in some time this week-Mr. J. Bruce Walker, for the Minister of the Interior, wrote a letter on the 31st day of July to the elevator people saying that when the homesteader brought in his grain the elevators were to grab as the first grab out of that grain, enough to pay the Government. Those are the homesteaders my hon. friends opposite are helping! That letter reads as follows:
Department of the Interior, Immigration Branch.
Winnipeg, July 31, 1915.
Sir,-The seed grain or other advances made to you by the Dominion Government in the winter of 1911-15 are, under the terms of the mortgage agreement entered into by you and the legislation governing the transaction, payable at the time the crop grown during the year 1915 is sold. I am therefore directed to notify you that the amount of such advances is required to be paid when you market this season's crop.
Arrangements have been made by the Government with' the respective grain purchasing interests and railway companies (these being the agents of the Government for this purpose) under which there will be set off or secured against the proceeds of the grain marketed by you the amount due by you. The a-ceipt of the elevator representative or the member of the Grain Growers' Association or other licensed grain buyer, or of the railway company (which will endorse the amount payable ' to the Government on the bill of lading in the case of grain shipped by the grower before sale) will be delivered to you and will be evidence that you are entitled to a discharge of the lien or mortgage. These receipts will be on forms furnished by the Government to the grain purchasing and shipping interests. Information as to the amount of the .advances and particulars of the location of the land charged with payment will be in the possession of these respective interests at the points at which you market your crop.
I am, sir,	>
.
Your obedient servant,
J. Bruce Walker,
For the Minister of the Interior.

It was no trouble for this Government to make an arrangement with the big elevator companies, and the railways, to act as their agents. This seed grain, and these coals, and this relief work, had all been extended to men who were at death's door from starvation a year ago. They had not a cent left with which to buy anything; they had -nothing but debts, and this beneficent, parental Government of which the Solicitor General is such an active member, a Government which has millions of dollars to see flow away to the blood-suckers, and verm-in around here, making themselves rich- it says to the poor homesteader who is trying -to make -a -country for us in Canada, an-d to develop our -resources: You bring your grain in to our ifrifin-ds and. agents, the railway eompiainies and the big elevator companies, and we have written to our friends -and -agents to grab the first bushel, or ten bushels, or one hundred bushels, and let your children go hungry, your wives unclothed, and your houses unwarmed, until we get paid. That is the true honest story of it, and I do not care whether I were a supporter of Sir Robert Borden or not, I say that is an outrage. Is there a man opposite who will say it is not an outrage? If these people [DOT] were worth helping as a charge on and an asset of our country, it was the greatest suicide to strangle them and put them out of business as soon as they had a chance to get on their feet. It was bad business, as well as being lacking altogether in the humane element.
When that came out I sent a long telegram-I remember it cost me $4 or $5. I paid for it because I did not think that a Government that has to take the last cent from a homesteader would pay for it. I sent it right to the Prime Minister, I did not fool with anybody else. That telegram was as follows:
Moosejaw Sask., Sept 4, 1915. Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden,
Prime Minister,
Ottawa, Ont.
Interior Department threatening to force payment by homesteaders for advances made by the Dominion Government last winter. This seems unreasonably drastic. Advances often made in former years and no such exacting requirements, and never was understanding under which advances accepted this year. As Federal representative of district most vitally concerned, I earnestly request your immediate and favourable consideration with view to withdrawal of such drastic orders. Considering total losses of last year, present low markets and unaccommodating attitude of banks, homesteaders cannot finance if Government exacts its pound of flesh, and result will be another
year of pitiful privation for homesteaders and their families. Surely this is not the year to coerce loyal and devoted citizens who are the chief factor in development and prosperity of our country.
That is signed W. E. Knowles and marked paid. I did not get any answer until the 8th, when I got this answer from the Prime Minister. He was afraid that I would get a little credit in this matter. I could anderstand, perhaps, my hon. friend from Souris thinking that. The reply was as follows:
Telegram received; Minister of Interior has already given consideration to subject

It took him four d-ays to tell me that. I do not belieye Sir John Macdonald, or Sir Wilfrid Laurier, or Sir John Thompson, would have taken the trouble to wire an ordinary back bencher that he had already attended to it, that -his wiring had had no success, and -that he had spent his four or five dollars for nothing.
Telegram received; Minister of Interior has already given consideration to subject and arrangements have been made which I think will be regarded satisfactory.
(Sgd.) R. L. Borden.
However, his wire came along showing that it had been done. I am glad that I received the wire because nobody knew it had been done until long after my wire was sent. I do not doubt the Prime Minister's word, but, of course, he has a great many things on his mind, and I think he has got a little mixed on the sequence of events. I very much question if it had been all fixed with -the Minister of Interior because it was three days after my wire had been sent forward that the announcement came that they were going to be content with the collection of -half of the seed grain advance. After having got that wire of mine-I do not say that it influenced their decision

but having got that wire, they decided that they would only take half of it this year. But, you will be sorry to know that a man who is so unfortunate as to have a judgment against him, and the sheriff goes after him, must submit to having it all taken from him. The poor chap whc- is in difficulties, and whose possessions the Sheriff is seizing, is placed in a most unfortunate position; the Government is taking every cent that is due by him, they are exacting their pound of flesh from him, I am going to prove it. Here is a letter from Mr. Charles H. Beddoe, superintending accountant, Department of the Interior, addressed to the sheriff, saying, that if a



seizure has been made this concession to let half of the thing go until next year does not apply, but that he must take every cent out of the poor fellow who has a judgment against him. The letter is as follows:
Ottawa, Jan. 8, 1916.
J. Rutherford, Sheriff,
Moosejaw, Sask.
Re Dominion Seed Liens and Liens for relief.
Dear Sir,-In reply to your favour of December 30, regarding' the above, I beg to advise you that the ruling of the department in regard to seizures, is, that the full amount of the Government's indebtedness must be provided for in full.
While the Government is satisfied to collect one-half of the seed grain account in all cases [DOT]where the security is in no way impaired, and the crop not interfered with, this does not apply where seizure has been made. Therefore, I will like your office to see that the total amount of indebtedness is collected. Unless in cases where half or part have been paid I will then advise you of the balance owing, which must be collected and remitted to this office.
I trust that you will regard the above instructions as being specific and entirely satisfactory to your office. Thanking you for your co-operation, I am,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.)Chas. H. Beddoe, Superintending Account.
Does my hon. friend not think- that instead of helping out the wealthy milling interests and the grain operators, he might have had some humanity in his heart and done something for the poor homesteader who has worked year after year, who is unavoidably the victim of an execution, who has a judgment registered against him, whose wife and little children have never had a cent spent on them for two or three years, and who has had to get credit for clothes, school books, and fuel to warm his house? But this Government said to this poor homesteader:	If you are so unfortunate as to have the sheriff after you, we shall come and take every accursed cent, besides costs and everything from you, and we will not make any concession to you. The man in the department, Charles H. Beddoe, who, under instructions, wrote that accursed, inhuman order, had no bowels of compassion whatever.

I may say to my hon. friend that the letter which he has quoted was, I toelieve, written on a misinterpretation of a departmental letter, and that as soon as it was brought to the notice of the Department of the Interior, I believe that the interpretation was corrected, and that no difference is made at all in such a case.
I accept that as being so; hut there is no doubt that it was acted on for months out there.
No.
Until a considerable time after I left Moosejaw it was acted on, because this was forwarded to me from Moosejaw a few days ago, and no letter had been sent to correct it up to that time.
That is the only case that was forought to the attention of the department that I know of.

I accept the statement that it was brought to the attention of the department, but why should the Government squeeze and persecute, and inhumanely treat these poor homesteaders, and say that they should get from them as much as possible, and that they .should refrain from doing this when it is brought to their attention? There is nothing to show that the sheriff acted on any representations from the department to the contrary, and I will be very much surprised if the Government has not a lot of money in its coffers collected from this source. I will be glad to find that the money collected has been sent .back to the homesteaders. But, in view of the harm that was done by the course that was pursued by the department, the Solicitor General _now comes forward and says something about a misinter-fpretation. Misinterpretation fiddlesticks. They realize that they made a mistake. If they could have got away with it; if they could have got away with the homesteader's money, we would not have heard anything about misrepresentation. The Government do not make mistakes that hurt the manufacturers, but they do make mistakes that hurt the homesteaders. They would not make any great mistakes affecting the manufacturers, the wheat operators or the millers. *
Has the hon. gentleman any information as to how much was paid back at the end of the year of this $15,000,000? I understand about $1,000,000.
I could not say as to that. The Government did all they could to have it paid back and it was not for lack of trying that they did not get the last drop of blood.
That is not correct.

They were trying to get every cent, and if I cam do 'anything to

prevent them from bleeding the home-'steader I will do it.
That is your business.

Yes, that is my business. I wish it was my hon. friend's business, and if he realized his position he would make it his' business.
There are certain problems that confront us that I wish to refer to and I say again that. I am sorry that the Minister of the Interior is not here. The greatest problem in this country, during and after the war, will be the problem of producing wealth. We are taking on very heavy financial responsibilities and liabilities. We are going to lose a great many of our producers. The country is going to be very severely strained in many ways and it is for us today to consider how we can replace this national loss by promoting national production. The production of wealth in this country has to come out of the soil. We have the productions of our mines, forests, fisheries and things of that kind but in the last resort our wealth must come out of the soik Before this war started when we are of course, under an abnormal condition of affairs,-and it bas been that very much since, although not so much now- there was not a town or city in the east or the west-and I will speak now more particularly of the west-in which you could not find men by the hundreds and thousands who could not get work. I could take you on trains and trails in almost any back township and I could show you millions upon millions of acres of land unused and producing nothing.
The problem of Canada is to bring together these men wiho are crying for work, and the land that is crying out to be worked. That is our national problem. You may call it a Western problem, but it is not a Western problem; it is a Canadian problem, and not a Liberal problem any more than a Conservative problem. We have millions and millions of acres crying out for men to go and cultivate them, and we have great numbers of men crying out for work, though not so many to-day as before the war,-and the problem of Canada is to bring these two together. Then you will have a great and wealthy Canada. When the Liberals were in power-I do not say it was because the Liberals were in power-these men wanting work, and the land wanting men, were brought together. Three or four years ago that all stopped, like a broken-down Ford automobile, and
28*
it has not gone on again since. The land is crying out for men, the men are there, but the two are not being brought together. It may be a joking matter to some hon. gentlemen opposite, but what made Canada great during the fifteen years the Lauriei Government was in power was that these two were brought together. I do not say it was the Laurier Government that made Canada great, but the men and the land were brought together, and national wealth was produced and we had a rich Dominion; and until these two can be brought together again Canada is not going to develop. What is going to bring them together? That is for the Government to decide. We on this side of the House thought and we still think in our humble way that conditions must be so fa- ourable and inviting that the men would be attracted to the land and become wealth-producing citizens. We tried to bring about these conditions by open markets, by reducing the taxation, by encouraging immigration, and by the Railway Commission. We tried in every way to encourage men to settle on the land. For four years now those conditions have not prevailed. I am not going to make a party speech.	,
Oh, oh!

I could make my speech a great deal hotter if I liked. If the Government does not think our way of bringing these two factors together is right, in Heaven's name let them tell us what is their way. The land should not be allowed to remain idle when we have railways, elevators, and steamships to take the grain out. We should not remain at standstill. We want to grow, and especially so in these times when we are assuming such large national obligations. The Minister of Finance would be doing a great work if he could solve this problem of bringing the men and the land together. If every acre was made to produce $16 or $25 annually we should have a wealthy Canada compared with what we now have, for there are millions of acres idle. I say that it is a problem for the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of the Interior to solve. If 1 were Minister of Interior I think I would tax those men who own land and arc not using it, say twenty-five cents an acre, or fifty cents, or a dollar an acre, any amount that would make them get rid of the land or hire a man to cultivate it. That is what the land is there for. Surely some method could be devised of making it too expensive for a man to hold

idle land. Perhaps a commission could solve the problem, though Heaven knows we have commiseionis enough. There must be knighthoods to spare, and if a commission could make a success of the job, we could afford to make them knights, or honorary colonels.- The greatest problem in Canada is how to use the soil that the Creator has given us. When we have solved that, there will be no trouble in financing the country. The Liberal party's solution of this problem was not accepted by the people of Canada. The present Administration does not think well of that solution, and it is therefore up to them to say what is the proper way to bring about the condition of affairs that we stated our policy would bring about. And in the meantime-I do not think this is a partisan statement to make-the responsibility is on the Government that such a vast amount of land is lying idle.

Mr. Speaker, -as this is the first opportunity I have had of addressing the House since you have been elevated to the position of first Commoner in Canada, I wish to take this opportunity of tendering to you my congratulations. I feel satisfied that in the discharge of your duties you will be absolutely fair and unpartisam, which is all that any one can demand from the Speaker of this House. While I do not hope that you 'should stay in your office too long, I do hope that you may stay there until there is a change of Government.
The speech of His Royal Highness the Governor General deals with two matters only: the extension of the term of Parliament, and the war. I would have thought that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and the men behind him, would have considered the carrying on of the war to a successful issue the most important question that this Parliament has to deal with at the present time. But the Prime Minister puts war in the second place, -and the extension of the life of Parliament in the first place. I suppose that keeping himself and his party in power so much longer was of more importance to the Prime Minister and his party than the carrying on of the war to a successful conclusion.
I shall deal with these two questions in reverse order, which is, I think, their proper order. As I have said on the two previous occasions we have met here during the war, we on this side of the House stand shoulder to shoulder with the Government in anything that pertains to the 
proper carrying on of this war. We told the Government last year that if the $150,000,000 we voted did mot carry them through, we would be ready to vote whatever further amount was needed. We said plainly on both those occasions that while we were voting laTge sums of money we did not intend to relinquish the right that every Opposition member, and every private member has of criticising the .manner iin which this money was being spent, and that we would hold the Government to account for the proper expenditure of that money. I do not think any hon. gentleman opposite can take exception to that position. I know that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister will not take any exception to that position, because he said that it was all right. But what do we find now? As soon as any effort is made to have an investigation of any kind in connection with the carryings on of the war, hon. gentlemen opposite undertake to lecture us and to tell us that we have no right to criticise the Government as we are doing, and that we are endeavouring to hinder them in the conduct of the war. My hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) the other day read us a great lecture about our action in criticising the Government, and he tried to make out that we were doing our best to force an election. During this debate I have not heard one word about an election, or about the forcing of an election. Why then did the hon. member from Peterborough wax' so indignant at us? Where was his indignation last year and the year before, when my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) was doing his utmost to drive the Government and the country into a general election? It was far more objectionable to consider an election then, practically in the middle of a term, when only three sessions of Parliament haa been held, than it is to-day when we are practically at the end of a parliamentary term, and when we are holding our fifth session. But there was no indignation on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite then. They thought there was going to be an election. Why was the Bill giving votes to our soldiers put through if hon. friends opposite had not thought of bringing on an election? Why did the Minister of Public Works make a speech down in Montreal
Eractically announcing that there was to e an election, and when he took the opportunity of handing out a gratuitous insult to a large number of the clergy qf the

Dominion of Canada? On those occasions no one on the other side of the House said anything at all against bringing on an election. Then it was all right; but now, when nobody on this side is saying a word about an election, when all we are doing is asking for an investigation into the expenditure of the Government, hon. gentlemen opposite, because they do not want to have the accounts looked into and investigated, say:	Oh, you are trying to
force the country into an election. Was anything ever further from the truth than that? We stand here to-day just as much in favour of supporting the Government in the carrying on of this war as we ever were. We are deeply involved in the war, and things have not been going as well as might have been expected or as many of us hoped, but we are into the war, and we are in it to stay until the end, cost what it may in men or in money. That is the position the Liberal party has taken, and that is the position we are going to stand by until the end of this war.
When the Prime Minister gave out a message on New Year's day calling for
500,000	men from Canada, he was only echoing the sentiments that have been advocated by many people in Canada during the past year. It was nothing new. Mr. Rowell, leader of the Opposition in Ontario, had advocated the same thing for many months. While I do not think it will be possible to get 500,000 men under the voluntary system, still it may be, and I hope it will be; but if we are going to succeed in getting 500,000 men, the Government will have to adopt very different tactics from what they have used in the past. The greatest hindrance to volunteering in the last year and a half has been the action and the words of the Minister of Militia. Time and again when I have been going through the country, I have said, when talking to young men:	"well, why have
you not volunteered to help the Empire?" " Well," the young man would say, " why should I? I have a good job and am getting good pay'; why should I offer to go when the Minister of Militia says that for every man they want there are two and three volunteering?" Ever since the war started, the Minister of Militia has been taking credit to himself for the manner in which he is conducting the raising of an army. In this way he has prevented hundreds and thousands of young men from joining the army, and at the same time that the Minister of Militia was making
these statements, thousands, and tens of thousands, and hundreds of thousands of dollars were being spent in the endeavour to secure troops. If you want men why not say so at once, and then you will have some chance of enlisting them. When the minister makes statements such as he did, it savours a good deal of partyism. He wanted to take some party advantage from it. There should be no partyism in the army. There is no partyism in the ranks. The Government is just as glad to get Liberals to fight in the ranks as to get Conservatives, I think it will be found throughout the country that at least as good a proportion of Liberals are volunteering for the trenches as are the Conservatives. One hon. member undertook, last year, to state on a platform that ninety to ninety-five per cent of the men who were going to the trenches belonged to the Conservative party. I characterize that statement as an absolute falsehood, and that hon. gentleman was forced to retract his words before he could leave that platform.
I know of one settlement that is practically almost all Liberal, a Scotch settlement, and in that whole settlement there is only one man of military age who is not wearing the King's uniform. And in face of tha-t, for a man to say that ninety to ninety-five per cent of the men in the trenches belong to the Conservative party is not the way to deal with recruiting. Does this Government expect to get volunteers if such statements are made? I trust that in the future the Minister of Militia will put a little grip on that tongue of his, because it is very apt to Tun away with him, and I hope that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister in the future will take a greater part in military matters than simply acting as a balance wheel for the erratic actions of the Minister of Militia. It was not I who said that the Prime Minister was a balance wheel; it was the Minister of Militia himself who made that statement, and I am only quoting his words.
I would like to ask my right hon. friend why the large number of vacant constituencies in Parliament have not been filled, some of which have been vacant for quite a long time? Are these seats not to be filled, and especially when the Prime Minister is coming down to ask for an extension of the time of Parliament? Why should these constituencies be disfranchised during this session? This is a rather serious matter. We are badly enough handicapped by still

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I had been making a few remarks about the loans that had been effected by the Government. I stated that I was very pleased to see the Finance Minister borrowing money both in Canada and in the United States. I think in that way we can help Great Britain in this waT a great deal better than by continuing as we have done in the past, to borrow in [DOT]Great Bnitian alone. I pointed out that we were paying a fairly high rate for the money, but I have learned since then that we are paying even more. I understand now that bonds have been issued for $100,000,000, and that these bonds can be exchanged, during a certain period, for forty years bonds at five per cent. I understand from the minister's gesture that that is not exactly right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The notes issued in New York for one or two years are exchangeable at the option of the holder for twenty year bonds.

I am glad to hear that, because that is much better than forty year bonds. I do not object so -much to five per cent or five and-a-half per cent to our own people, but I trust, if the minister goes to the United States for more money-and I think it would be good policy to borrow in the United States if wc? can get the money at the Tight rate-he will be able to secure more favourable terms. I -see that the state of New York has borrowed money within the past few days at 3-80 per cent. The securities of Canada ought to be as good, I think, as the security of the state of New York. I trust that the Finance Minister, in making future loans, will be able to make a good bargain, and that he will have lots of trucking and trading with the Americans if he can borrow -money cheaper there than he can any place else.

* I would ask the Minister of Public Works to bring to the attention of the Minister of Militia a matter which I wish to bring before this House. My information is- and I get this information from an officer in Canada who ought to know what he is talking about-that in the ordinary battalions stationed in Canada full rations are drawn every day for the number of men in the battalion. If a battalion is at full strength, with a thousand men, they draw their rations daily for qne thousand men. I am informed that in the average battalion throughout the country, through leave of absence and one thing or another, from ten. per cent to twenty per cent of the men are not at headquarters-but the rations are drawn just the same. So the people of Canada are paying for those rations, whether the men are there or not; and in the opinion of this officer this amounted to about $500 a week in the case of many battalions, which would represent $2,000 per month for each battalion. If we have one hundred battalions at $2,000 per month, there you have $200,000 per month, or $2,400,000 per annum. Where does that money go? If the men are not at headquarters they can not use the rations, but yet the rations are charged up in full. I do not know that that is an absolutely correct statement, but that is the statement I have from an officer of the force who knows his duty, who is a good soldier, and who assured me that his statement to me is an absolute fact which can be verified by the department very, very easily. If that is the case, surely to goodness such a state of affairs should be stopped.

An affair of that kind could not possibly exist in a battalion which is run properly, because the rations are requisitioned by the quartermaster every morning. If you had a dishonest quartermaster it mfiighit occur, but it could not occur in the regiments generally.

If that state of affairs
exists it must be by connivance between certain officers and contractors. After what we have heard in connection with shell contracts, I do not know that it would be beyond belief that perhaps some of the contractors who are furnishing the supplies might not be above making some money over and above a legitimate profit. However, I bring the matter to the attention of the Government and hope it will be investigated; and, if it is found that the

statement is well founded, that the abuse will be put a stop to.
My attention was also directed, by an officer who has been overseas and has been through many battles, to a statement that the medical examination in Canada is hardly worthy the name of inspection, and that hundreds and hundreds of men have gone overseas who should never have been allowed to pass. They have been drilled, and fed, and paid for from six months to fifteen months before being sent over. Then, after experiencing the discomfort of the trenches, and the other discomforts, altogether apart from the danger, they get tired of the trench life, they trot out this trouble, whatever it is, that should have been detected in the first place by the medical examination; they are unfit according to the law and they should never have been sent to the front. They are tired of the whole business and they want to be sent home, and they are sent home at a cost of probably $1,000 or $2,000 per man. They come home, and in many cases they will demand and will secure pensions. There is no doubt that this has happened and is happening. It is a matter of great importance that should he looked into. We will have tens of thousands of men to look after through our pension office when the time comes; but why should we have men who are taken over there through the absence of proper medical inspection, and who, as soon as they get tired of soldiering, show up their defects and are sent home to become a charge on the country, and to remain so, many of them, as long as they live. To my mind, it is a most serious matter and one thoroughly well worth looking into. If it be the case, as I know it is the case, a stop should be put to it at once. Let us send no more unfit men overseas; let us send only fit men to bear the brunt of the fight, because it is only a waste of money to send the unfit.
That brings me to the question of pensions. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Marine (Mr. Hazen) speak as he did in connection .with pensions. In my judgment that will be one of the most important phases of the war that we as a Parliament will have to deal with; there will be a great many men who will be entitled to claim a pension from the Government, and it would seem that the matter should be removed, as suggested by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, entirely out of the hands of politicians in any shape or form. You know that there will be 300,000 or

400,000 coining back from the war and they will be a big power in the country. They will probably represent one-fifth, or one-seventh, of the voting power of Canada, and it seems to me of the utmost importance that the subject of pensions should be dealt with early by absolutely independent men, or by a department as long as it is properly dealt with that it should be gone into thoroughly and quickly, and that a decision should be arrived at that will be fair to the men, the officers and the relatives who have been left behind by those who have lost their lives in the war. The whole matter should be settled once and for all so that we will not find ourselves in the position of the United States which, fifty years after the war, is paying a larger sum in pensions that it was paying many years ago. With regard to the sums that are now being paid according to the schedule, it seems to me that there has been too wide a difference between the private and the officer. However, I am not in a position to take that subject up and I am quite sure it will be dealt with by whoever may handle the pension fund. My main point is that whatever is done should be done quickly so that there will be no complication that can be avoided.

In every case where, during last session, the Opposition undertook to bring any matter up for investigation, either before the Boots Committee or the Public Accounts Committee, it was shown that they were absolutely justified in all the state-

ments they had made, it was proven that there had been a great deal of wrong-doing, and since then the Militia Department and the Government have been buying their supplies, boots, drugs, horses and everything else at much better prices and more in the interest of the country than before these investigations took place. If good resulted from the investigation of these matters last year, why should it not be beneficial this session, and why should there not be an investigation?
We have heard a good deal in the last five years about patriotism and loyalty. Is it patriotic or loyal to charge Canada and the British Empire $5.70 for doing the work that we now have done for $1.75, and which can be done at a profit for $1? You would have thought, Sir, that this Government would have wanted to supply *shells and other munitions of war cheaply, and as there were four or five hundred million dollars worth of contracts to be let, that they would have organized a department to look after the manufacture of shells, and find out just what they cost to produce. Did they do it? No. They said they would *do it when they were asked by Mr. Thomas, the man Lloyd George sent out, and they got credit all over the country for their patriotism in placing these shops at the disposal of the Empire at the eleventh hour. A good many people believe, and I would like to believe myself, that the war will be over in another year. Unfortunately we have no proof of that.
It is only a supposition; it may occur or it may not. That subject is worthy of consideration by the Government and the Government should take action on it. mestic matters. This Government is not toying to practise economy. My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) says ten times, but I am going to be within the mark and I will put it at six times. That is only in line with all of the actions of the Government in their dealings with the farmers. How does it come that you can ship a car load of wheat from Regina, Calgary, Brandon, or Portage la Prairie, to Winnipeg and down to Fort William over the Canadian Pacific Railway at exactly the same rate as you could two years ago before the war started? There is no difference. Why? Because we control the rates on the railways in Canada. As soon as that wheat strikes the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers at Montreal they charge us as much to-day for one car of wheat as they charged for six cars two years ago.
Simply because we cannot control the rates.

My hon. friend says
that, but last year, when the Canadian Pacific Railway charter was up for discussion in this House I moved the following amendment:
That the following clause be added to the Bill as clause 6 :
That the freight rates charged by the companythat is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company who were asking for a new( charter for their boats.

shall be subject to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
The Minister of Public Works and all his colleagues, would not accept that and de-' feated it. Therefore, we have no control of the rates at the present time, and, therefore, we are paying from six to ten times as much to get a bushel of wheat from Montreal to Liverpool as we did prior to the opening of the war. The previous year a new charter wiais granted to the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation. Company. On that occasion we on this side of the House, and, to their credit, some hon. gentlemen opposite, tried to induce the Government to put that and other companies under the direction of the Railway Commission, which would regulate their issue of securities, freight rates, and other matters. The majority of hon. gentlemen opposite, however, refused to support us, and the result is that on the lakes to-day we have freight rates three or four times as high as before the war. Has the war made shipping on the lakes any more dangerous, thereby causing insurance rates to go up? No.

Owing to the refusal of hon. gentlemen opposite these inland and ocean lines are able to do anything they like in the way of robbing the farmer of a legitimate price for his wheat.
What proportion of the export grain of the Northwest passed through Buffalo during the past year?

I cannot give my hon.
friend the exact figures, but it would be a very large amount.
I am told it was about eighty per cent. How could the shipment of this grain to Buffalo be caused by the rates on Canadian vessels, when the bulk of it was carried by American vessels?

Why should this grain
not go via Buffalo when it cost such a high rate to take it from Montreal? Had the freight rates been lower on the St. Lawrence route, more wheat would have gone that way'. Another reason that accounts for this grain going from Buffalo was the commandeering of the wheat by this Government a month ago. Dealers do not want to be put in the position they were in then, of having their wheat taken from them, and being unable to fill contracts. In order to take no chances they shipped via the United States rather than via the St. Lawrence.
There is no difference between the two routes.

Instead of commandeering the wheat, wha't might this Government . have done? The lake and rail rate to Montreal during the fall was thirteen cents a bushel. That price would enable the Transcontinental Railway to land the wheat in St. John, N.B., or in Halifax, or in Portland, Maine, and make a big profit. It would have made about ten thousand dollars per train from Winnipeg to Portland, or to St. John. There was an opportunity to do something for the railroads, but the Government did not take advantage of it. And they could have helped not only the railroads, but the farmers, too, to the extent of six or ten cents a bushel. Some time during the month of November last I was in. Estevan, in my constituency. I went on the market, and found that farmers were getting eighty-four cents a bushel for their wheat, but when it was loaded on the car, if it was available at once, they could get ninety-four cents a bushel. That is, there was a difference of ten cents a bushel between the track price and the street price. The Government could have bought the

They commandeered the wheat, and did the farmer out of his legitimate gains, in order that my hon. friends the Solicitor General and the Minister of Public Works might make a political scoop. It was done to stem the rising tide of a demand for free wheat.	.

Those in a position to

My hon. friend may not like it, because he will have his difficulties in explaining to his constituents the action of his friend the Solicitor General.
And the St. Peters affair.

This will be much worse than the St. Peters affair. Every other hon. gentleman who supports the Government in commandeering that wheat will have some explaining to do before the electors. This shows very clearly how differently the Government treats the manufacturer as compared with the farmer. Mr. Speaker, allow me at the outset to add my congratulations to you on your elevation to the Speakership. At this particular time, which is unparalleled in Canada's history, even although this debate which has lasted for some days may seem somewhat prolonged, it is our duty, seeing that we sit here as representatives of Canadian constituencies, and that we are all practically of Canadian birth, to offer what suggestions we may to the Government of this country in this time of stress. In view of what has been done by the citizenhood of the Dominion of Canada-and may I in that respect mention especially the women of the Dominion-there are two duties incumbent on the parties in this House.
The duty of the Government is to give the lead to patriotic public sentiment; to sacrifice all other considerations in the determination to make Canada's share in the struggle a worthy and effective one; to banish sternly and rigorously the petty and often costly intrigues of mere party politics, and the reprehensible and dishonest tactic3 of get-rich-quick-at-the-country's-expense middlemen. It is further the duty of the Government to invite friendly counsel and thoughtful and honest criticism; to legislate with an eye single to the speedy accomplishment of the great task of the Empire; to deal resolutely with every instance of impropriety brought to its attention, by searching public investigation, and to further improvement in methods wherever they have been shown to be faulty.
There is also a duty that devolves upon us as the Opposition party in this House. It is, to give sympathetic and hearty support and assistance to the Government in all legislation making for the attainment of the national and imperial objects immediately in view; to pass with the utmost freedom and despatch all war grants and all bills designed to make more effectual Canada's part in the conflict; to bring promptly and frankly to the Government's attention all cases of impropriety or worse, that may come to its attention, and to urge full investigation, and, wherever possible, restitution. It is as well, Sir, the duty of the Opposition to aid the Administration with helpful counsel and suggestion; to put aside for the time being mere party criticism and devote its energies solely to its foremost responsibility at this hour-to see to it, so far as may be in its power, that the full measure of the service and sacrifice of the people is applied in the most direct, honest, and efficient manner, to the patriotic purpose for which it has been so heartily given.
These appear to me to be the outstanding duties of the members of this House. I do not here desire to make any protestations of loyalty; these are unnecessary. I firmly believe that, with the exception .of the leaders of the Nationalist party, there is not a disloyal man of Canadian birth in Canada. I believe that we are all loyal, that we are all doing what we can in the great cause to which all our energy should be directed. Let me point out in passing, that even Bourassa, with all that he would have us believe of Canada and of the British Empire, has his practical views of this matter. When the war broke out, by the strange irony of fate, he was in France, the home of his fathers, and immediately upon the declaration of war he was one of the fiTst 'to jump aboard a British boat and under the British flag come back to Canada. That was Bourassa. He may not admire this country, he may have hard things to say of the British Empire, but the fact remains-for his actions speak louder than words-than when he desired- to save his own hide the British flag was good enough for him.
It has been said, Sir, that Canada- in this war has found her soul. There is this much to be said of Canada and Canadians: that more than ever before have they been brought to a greater sense of their responsibilities and of Canada's position as a part of the British Empire. Canada's responsibilities are no longer nebulous or theoretical. If we desire to remain a part of this

great British Empire and of that I have not the slightest doubt, and I pray God we may so remain-our duties are plain, our duties are concrete; Canadians must rise to a greater sense of responsibility than that to which they have hitherto attained.
The Government of Canada has passed through twenty months of happenings such as no Government in this country ever passed through before. They have met their responsibilities, in some cases well, in some cases not so well. But though great questions have arisen heretofore in the course of this war, greater questions are going to arise shortly after the close of the war; questions that will call for consideration by the whole Canadian people; questions that must be looked square in the face and in the light of day, especially by every man who takes upon himself the responsibilities of a representative of the people. The Government will have to face a period of reconstruction at the end of this war, and it will have problems to deal with that will call for men, strong, courageous, and irrespective of party, with an eye single to duty.
Our debt to-day is enormous; it is rapidly growing and will be very much greater at the close of this war.' That debt must be met and taxation applied therefor in a way that shall be as equitable as possible. In levying that taxation and making provision for the payment of that debt, my own opinion is that the men of great wealth in this country-to preserve which wealth great sacrifices have been made, much blood shed, and enormous treasure given- when that final reckoning comes, the responsibility of these men who have been so greatly taken care of should not be overlooked.
Another problem that will confront us at the close of this war is the home-coming soldier, and that is a problem, with one other I shall mehtion, that, above all others, the people of Canada, if they dare to call themselves loyal citizens, if they have faith in themselves and in the Empire, must take care of. To my mind, it is the State's most sacred and bounded duty to see to it that these men, when they shall return, whether whole or maimed, shall find just provision .madie for them as for men who sacrificed their all, and by the shedding of their blood shed such lustre upon Canada.
Then there is the pension scheme, and that is the other problem that I refer to, as being, with the problem of the returned 
soldier, the greatest that we have to deal with. We mourn for those who have lost their lives in defence of the honour of this country, and for the maintenance of liberty, justice, and civilization,. The dependents of these men, the widow and the orphan, should be protected in such a way that no man can look a Canadian in the faoe and say that we have not done our full duty to honour the memory of those who have given everything for Canada. We who remain at home have lived and are living, even during war, in peace, comfort and happiness. True, many of the homes of this country have been rendered sad by the loss of those who were most near and dear, and therefore it is that I say, that as through their efforts and their sacrifices we have enjoyed a period of prosperity 'and happiness in this country, they having lost their lives in this war, leaving dependents behind them a pension 'scheme must be devised by whatever Government that may be in power that will be absolutely fair and will amply provide for those who are dependent upon it.
Another matter that will require attention When this reconstruction takes place is the land question. Peradventure a great flood of immigration should come to this country from the war-ravished lands of Europe after the conflict is over, and a land scheme should be devised for the soldiers who return, on the basis of actual settlement upon the land. I am not in favour of issuing scrip as a bonus, as has been done heretofore; the land should be given to the returned soldiers upon the condition and understanding that they should become actual settlers upon it; that they should cultivate it, and that no title might be made, by way of giving speculators a chance, within five years of the granting of the patent, or at least until the death of the patentee. I think some such system ought to be evolved. It appears to me that these are some of the few problems that will have to be faced; in my humble way they strike me as being important; I give them to the House for what they are worth.
Another matter that will require consideration is improved defences both_ by land and by water. I do not believe that there will ever be such a thing as perpetual peace; I do believe that from now on such preparations will have to be made by every nation that hereafter no war may be brought about and carried on as this one has been. I believe that the only way

to prevent such an occurrence is by absolute and entire preparedness. There is no doubt about the fact that at the present time Canada is passing through a period of transition. She is passing from a too self-satisfied, money-making people to a people who realize that they have left behind them the dependent stage, and, by sacrifice of blood and treasure, have passed into a great world of nations. We welcome this transition; we join in that nationhood with our heads up as self-reliant, courageous Canadians.
It has been broadly stated that there should be no criticism of the Government's action at this particular time. I am not inclined to agree with that view, although for the moment I do not intend to criticise to any considerable extent. I merely desire to say that wholesome criticism of any government is good. The Government should welcome any criticism that is honest and that will make for the betterment of the country in the present strenuous times. My genial friend the Minister of Public Works, for whom I have a great regard, sometimes exercises a rather fine Italian hand along these lines. I think that in some respects he has been endeavouring of late to manufacture a few more thunder tones for the country. I make that remark on account of an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Saturday Post of January 22, 1916. I understand that the policy of this paper is in some way controlled, or at least guided with a parental hand, by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works.

I am sure that my hon.
friend does rot wish to do me an injustice. I can assure him that I have no connection in any shape or form with the Winnipeg Saturday Post, and never had.

I am most delighted to
accept the hon. gentleman's explanation. However, the Winnipeg Saturday Post is a rather strong Conservative organ. It says:
The Opposition, since the beginning of the war, has professed ultra-loyalty and at the same time has done everything possible to give the impression that the Government has been remiss in its duty. Either the Government is at fault, or the Opposition is in error. The most expedient method of determining the correctness of the several attitudes involved is by making an appeal to the people. Precipitating a general election at the present time may justly be regarded as unfortunate, but it could not be so unfortunate as the condition that we have to-day, where an Opposition, while professing loyalty, is striving by every subtle means to handicap the Administration in its patriotic efforts to advance the British cause.	:
I take a decidedly opposite view to' that which is expressed in this article. As I have already said, honest criticism is good and the Government should welcome it. May I say to the Government and their supporters that if, by reason of the criticism which they have received during this session, they take it upon themselves to say that they have a mandate from the Canadian people to ask for their opinion at the polls, there will be no justification for that attitude; and if they do bring an election on, the blame will be entirely upon their own heads.
Do not be afraid, we do not intend to do it.

Surely it is not unjust
criticism to say that the Minister of Public Works might to-day, when all our resources ought to be conserved, do a little less spending in his department. Surely I might say also to my hon. friend the Minister of Cus-. toms that he refrain from taking on every man who wants a job, and thus curtail the expenditures in his own department and not increase them, as he has been doing. Surely we might say to the Postmaster General your revenue is decreasing and your expenditure is increasing. Why? Because Conservatives are out of jobs and want to be looked after. Surely it is right and proper to bring these matters to the attention of the Government. Surely we might say, Sir, to the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) that the people of the province of Ontario want to know why, with a tender in from T. Eaton & Company, of Toronto, for trousers at $3.20 a pair, the Capital Brand Trouser Company, of Toronto, were given a contract at $3.73 a pair, and that the people of the Dominion of Canada paid $40,000 more for the soldiers' trousers than they should have paid. Surely that is honest criticism. Is it not honest criticism also to ask the Government why Ellis & Ellis should have contracts for parts of shells when they are not in the shell-making business? These are all matters interesting ajt lelast to tihe people of the province of Ontario, and I do arrogate to myself the right to speak for some small portion of them. I say to the Government that these are things that must be cleared up. I say too, that the people demand the clearing up of these things; and I say further to the Government, that if they do not clear them up in a way that is satisfactory to the people of the province of Ontario, they will be deemed to have been remiss in the trusteeship of

the people of the Dominion of Canada which they are there to carry out. These are all things that must properly and thoroughly be explained to the people of the Dominion of Canada; and it is the bounden duty of this or any other Government to see that they are so explained.
There are so'me lessons to be drawn from this war, hard though they may have been to learn. The one lesson that strikes me and that I would ask those on the other side of the House to take to heart is that, the other day, the Minister of Militia in making his speech in this House in defence of his department, unconsciously I know, and utterly unwittingly, paid the members on this side of the House a tribute that essentially, at least to my mind, established the fact that when the Minister of Militia voted as he did vote against the naval scheme propounded by the Liberal party, he voted in a way that he knew was not in accordance with the dictates of his conscience; that he voted in that way for party purposes and party purposes only. At page 305 of Hansard the minister said, in answer to a question as to whether any shells were manufactured in Canada'before the war:
Yes, at tht arsenal at Quebec. About 75 shells per day was our output, and 75 per cent were bad.
Then, he went on, and, by easy stages, led up to what was being done in the way of the manufacture of shells by the Shell Committee; and he said, speaking of an occasion where Canadian soldiers were fighting:
Let me point out that on that occasion our boys were armed with Canadian rifles, shooting Canadian ammunition, and firing Canadian shells. Having no shells to Are on Thursday, General Morrison found on Friday afternoon that a shipment had come to one of the stations eight or nine miles back. He sent his wagons back and commandeered 8,000 shells, and found that they were Canadian. Then, on Friday evening and Saturday, Canadian riflemen, armed with Canadian rifles, firing Canadian ammunition, and Canadian artillery, firing Canadian shrapnel shells, held back upwards of one hundred thousand of the best soldiers the world has ever produced.
I would like to -ask my hon. friends on the other side of the House, and I would particularly -ask the Minister of Militia if he were here, if he would just transpose that a little bit and take himself back to the naval debate we had in this House but a few years ago; and then bring himself along again by easy stages until at this time he might have said to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries from his place in the House': Here we have what? adian boats, owned by Canadians, built in Canada, manned by Canadians, patrolling the Canadian coasts, convoying Canadian troops, protecting Canadian trade routes, with Canadian guns, firing Canadian ammunition and maintained by Canadian money. It does not appear to me that that is much of a step in advance of the concrete instance given to us by the [DOT]Minister of Militia the other day. To-day we might have had a naval reserve of thousands of men, and the British naval officers calling for men might go to the Great Lakes and to the sea coasts of Canada, east and west, where you have thousands of young men whose very home is the water, and who to-day would gladly enlist to help England's navy if she needs them-and she does need them. We should have had all that to-day had the scheme as originally laid down and as accepted by this House, backed by the last man. of the Opposition of this House, been carried out. Together with Canadian ammunition we would have had the nucleus of our Canadian navy, and not have had to depend on Japanese boats or Australian boats. We would have had the same sight as was given as an object lesson to those Canadians who had not in them the real pride of Canadianihood, that they were as good as any people under the sun. You would have had the same object lesson that was given by the Sydney, the Australian cruiser. The very words uttered by the Minister of Militia, to my mind, absolutely prove that contention. I sincerely trust as a Canadian that I shall never -again see the -spectacle presented by any Government in Canada, to the world or to our sister colonies, of a Government saying to Canadian mechanics and Canadian artisans, the best there are in the world: You are not good enough to do the work that other artisans and mechanics can do. They s-aid it only for -the purpose of hiding themselves behind the mantle of nationalism. That is why it was done. The old, old story again. I ishall not enlarge upon it, it would be impertinent on -my part after the, classic in those lines that the hon-. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) gave u-s the other day.
There is one -other thing as to which I purpose speaking. I approach the matter, I will confess, with some degree of hesitancy because along these lines, as along others, I trust I am a good enough Liberal to let every man have his own opinion; even if he does not -agree with me, his

opinion may be as good as mine, but we may not look at it in the same way. We rather pride ourselves on the fact-at least speaking for myself, I do-that this is a democratic Canada. We are young, we are big, and we are broad. We have great stretches of country that positively spell democracy.
It has become the fashion in this country to attempt to build up a sort of pseudoaristocracy. Upon every available occasion, when we take up the papers, we see a long list of titles. You positively stumble upon these knights in the streets. I met one of them the other day and I had forgotten for the time that an honour had been conferred t upon him- Presently he came around to it and, after preening himself very considerably he said: Oh yes, but you know, Fred, the women want it. That may be all very well, it may be true, but, Mr. Speaker, I have an idea in the back of my head that the women are put up to it by the men. Speaking in all seriousness, I jotted down a few moments ago such worldwide names as William Ewart Gladstone, John Bright, Richard Cobden, Herbert H. Asquith, Lloyd George, Edward Blake, George Brown, Alexander Mackenzie. Do you want better men than these? Would Blake, Brown, or Mackenzie, have been greater Canadian had they had prefixes and half the letters of the Alphabet after their names? They stood upon their merits as those merits were recognized by the Canadian people. I say, Sir, that for a young, democratic country, we have had enough of titles and that a man in Canada should be recognized for one thing and one thing only-the merit that there is in him and the good that he does to his fellow-men. Provided he is a Canadian gentleman it is a good enough title for anybody.
I want to say, in conclusion, that our Canadian soldiers have shown themselves to be equal to any in courage and in resourcefulness. The people of this country, especially the women, are doing their share, and it remains for the members of this House to be their equals in political courage and political morality.
